module_title: Functioning, Criticism, and the Fall of the Planning Commission
introduction: At this advanced level, we analyze why a powerful body that directed the nation's economy for 65 years was suddenly dissolved in 2014, and what structural flaws led to its demise.

core_concepts.title: Top-Down Approach
core_concepts.description: This was the biggest criticism of the Planning Commission. Policies were drafted by central experts sitting in Delhi and imposed uniformly across all states ('One Size Fits All'). This approach completely ignored the vast geographic and economic diversity of India (e.g., forcing the same agricultural plan on Kerala and Bihar).

core_concepts.title: Financial Allocation Powers
core_concepts.description: Although it was supposed to be an advisory body, over time, the Planning Commission acquired the immense power to 'allocate financial resources' to states and central ministries. This led to severe clashes with the Finance Ministry and forced state Chief Ministers to lobby in Delhi for funds.

core_concepts.title: Plan vs. Non-Plan Expenditure
core_concepts.description: The Commission divided the budget artificially. 'Plan Expenditure' (building new assets) was considered good, while 'Non-Plan Expenditure' (maintenance, salaries) was considered bad. This resulted in skewed development—schools were built (Plan expenditure), but there were no funds to paint them or pay teachers (Non-plan expenditure).

core_concepts.title: Dissolution and NITI Aayog
core_concepts.description: Due to these structural rigidities, the Government of India officially scrapped the Planning Commission on August 13, 2014. It was replaced by 'NITI Aayog' (National Institution for Transforming India) on January 1, 2015, which was designed purely as a 'Think-Tank' operating on the principle of 'Cooperative Federalism'.

important_entities.name: Current Status of NDC
important_entities.significance: Because the Governing Council of NITI Aayog already includes all Chief Ministers, the NDC became entirely redundant. While it has not been technically abolished by any order, it is practically dead, with no meetings held since 2012.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Financial Powers: PC vs. NITI Aayog
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: In statement-based questions, examiners often write: 'Like the Planning Commission, NITI Aayog has the power to allocate funds to states.' This is FALSE. NITI Aayog has been stripped of all financial allocation powers. That power now rests solely with the 'Ministry of Finance'.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: The Planning Commission wrongly assumed that the exact same economic strategy that works for industrialized Gujarat will also work for the hilly terrain of Meghalaya.

exam_strategy_tips: The conceptual difference between the 'Top-Down Approach' (Planning Commission) and the 'Bottom-Up Approach' (NITI Aayog) is heavily tested in UPSC Prelims and Mains.
